questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Large and interesting city, English speaking university, recognized as a good university with good academic opportunities.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Didn't have any problems, as McGill is used to getting lots of exchange students.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't really need any, but there were plenty of options to receive assistance, if you needed help with anything in regards to signing up for courses, finding your way around campus etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was offered housing through McGill. I would not recommend this to others, as it was more expensive than private housing, exchange students living at the students residences had to pay for a mandatory meal plan, and I was placed together with an 18-year old freshman. Most other exchange students were placed together with other exchange students, but if you are one of the unlucky ones like me, it is definitely not worth the money to get housing through McGill's student housing services.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I would advise you to find your own housing and not accept any offers from McGill.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very lucky and got all the courses I wanted. However, this was not the case for most of the other Danish exchange students so be prepared for this.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
We were able to register before we went on exchange. Registration opens to exchange students later than for all other students, so although you are signing up for courses as soon as you are able too, there is no guarantee you'll get the courses you want. 
The first two weeks there is an "add and drop" period, where you can change your courses if there are available spots on other courses. Most exchange students were able to get courses they were more or less satisfied with.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: As an exchange student you were offered a conversation with a student counselor during the add and drop period. I did not need it, but I think it was helpful for the people who went.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can not necessarily expect to get exactly the courses you want. Prepare a list of more than four courses that you would be satisfied with and try to be open minded about which courses you end up taking.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had some really good courses and one awful course. My impression is that the level of the ECON-courses are lower than at UCPH so try to sign up for 500-level or honours courses if you are allowed to.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level of the courses really depend on the professor. If you are studying economics at UCPH, I would recommend you to take either 500-level courses, honours courses, or courses within other fields as my impression is that the level is generally lower than at UCPH if you take normal
ECON-courses.This
is primarily based on my experience from one 400-level course, so it is not necessarily correct for all economics courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
There were generally fewer people in each class, resulting in more interesting lectures with more interaction with the professor, which was nice. 
I had 3 hours of lectures (or 2 hours of lectures, 1 hour of conference) for each course (3 credit courses), which meant I had to study more independently from what I am used to at UCPH. 
The TAs are generally really nice and helpful - use them for all your questions regarding the courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ECON460: History of Thought I with Professor Green 
ECON546, Game Theory with Professor Dutta
ECON423, International Trade with Professor Karageusian 
POLI231, Political Theory with Professor Roberts.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Game Theory, History of Thought and Political Theory were all great courses. The professors were good and passionate about the courses, and I really learned a lot. I would especially recommend Game Theory with Professor Dutta to all economics students. However, be prepared that the workload of the courses is relatively big. 

International Trade was the worst course I have ever taken. I would not recommend it to anyone. Only good thing is that the course is relatively easy.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
As I lived at one of McGill's student residences I had to pay 1300 dollars for a mandatory meal plan at the beginning of my stay (on top of rent). 

I went to Boston, Toronto and Ottawa while I was here. All of the trips were relatively expensive, so if you're planning on visiting other cities, you should definitely leave some room for this in your budget.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
The CAD was really expensive when I first arrived, so everything was more expensive than expected. However the exchange rate improved while I was here, meaning everything suddenly seemed much cheaper. 
Montreal is not a cheap city to live in, and housing prices have risen, meaning housing is generally not as cheap as former travel reports suggest (although my rent was definitely higher than average).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Plenty of activities were available. 

I went on Outdoor Frosh when I arrived (I can really recommend it to all student on exchange here during the Fall Term, find "mcgilloutdoorsclub" or "mcgilloutdoorfrosh" on Instagram to read more about it). I also participated in a couple of McGill Outdoor Club's weekly meetings, which were always nice. 
McGill Athletics and Recreation has a nice gym (requires a cheap membership), a pool, and courts for badminton, basket, squash etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Outdoor Frosh, the facilities at McGill Athletics.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Toronto or Boston. Sign up for trips with Concordia Outdoor Club (more expensive than McGill, but much easier to get a spot). Go on outdoor trips/hikes.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: McGill is very international and great at welcoming exchange students.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I primarily spoke with other exchange students, as they were most eager to socialize.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Some of the people living in Montreal are not too friendly towards you if you don't speak French. In general Quebec has some weird language protection laws and the entire atmosphere around the language question would make me feel very unwelcome, if I were to move to Montreal more permanently. But you don't really experience anything in that regard at McGill at all, so I would still very much encourage everyone to go to McGill - even if you don't speak any French (I don't).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The culture and atmosphere at McGill is very nice. There are people from lots of different countries and cultures, and I learned a lot from that.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
McGill is a great university for exchange students - they are used to welcoming lots of exchange students every year, and they are great at making you feel welcome. 

You have to be a little bit proactive both in regards to finding friends, but also in regards to your courses. I was surprised by how different e.g. the exams are here. Reach out to your TAs and professors if you have questions for the courses - most of them are very helpful. 

Find your own housing - I would not recommend the housing offered by McGill. 

Also be aware that you are not the only one who is overwhelmed by having to arrange everything for your exchange. Most people who are going on exchange finds the process overwhelming at some point. Reach out to the other exchange students from Denmark going to McGill. They are probably searching for the answers of the same questions as you are. Help each other!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Apply for RAMQ as soon as possible - not everyone got it in time. 

Bring a SIM card for your phone from Denmark (I used CBB World). It is much more expensive here. 

Make sure your rejseforsikring covers the entire stay or buy an additional one (e.g. Europæiske Rejseforsikring, you get a discount as a member of DJØF). 

Apply for scholarships before you leave DK - otherwise the chance of getting any is very low.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the nice people I have met!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I really had to get used to how different it is to study here - e.g. when everyone had midterms and was kind of stressed out in the middle of the semester.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
